posts.title: Computer use is the real agent unlock
posts.hook: Everyone's building AI agents that call APIs. The ones that actually work navigate UIs.
posts.body:
Everyone's building AI agents that call APIs. The ones that actually work navigate UIs.

I have a QA step in my enrichment pipeline that requires clicking through a legacy CRM portal. No API. No export button. Just a 2004-era web form with session tokens that expire every 12 minutes.

Set up Claude computer use to handle it last week. It logs in, navigates three tabs, pulls the verification data, and writes it back to my SQLite enrichment table.

Took about 90 minutes to get the prompt right. The trick was screenshot-based checkpoints. You tell it "after clicking Submit, wait until you see the confirmation banner before proceeding." Without that, it races ahead and clicks on elements that haven't loaded yet.

The boring reality: computer use isn't replacing your dev team. It's replacing the 47 tabs you have open while manually bridging two systems that will never have a native integration.

Every GTM stack has at least one of these gaps. A portal that only works in Chrome. A partner dashboard with no API. A compliance check that lives behind a login wall.

That's where computer use actually lands. Not the demo. The gap.

remixes.hook: The most valuable automation I built this year doesn't touch a single API endpoint.
remixes.body:
The most valuable automation I built this year doesn't touch a single API endpoint.

It clicks buttons. It reads screen elements. It navigates a portal that was built before REST was a thing.

Here's the context: I have a verification step that requires cross-referencing data in a legacy CRM. The kind where you log in with a username that's also your employee ID, and the session dies if you open a second tab.

No one was going to build an API for this. The vendor hasn't shipped an update since 2019. The internal team gave me a PDF of "workarounds" that was basically "copy paste faster."

So I pointed Claude computer use at it. Took an afternoon to get the navigation reliable. Another hour to handle the session timeout loop. Now it runs every morning at 6am, pulls verification data, and writes it back to my pipeline before I open my laptop.

The ROI conversation around AI agents focuses too much on greenfield builds. The real money is in the systems nobody wants to touch. The ones with no documentation, no API, no export. Just a browser and a prayer.

Every company has at least three of these. Most have a dozen. That's where computer use stops being a demo and starts being infrastructure.
remixes.cta: What's the oldest, most neglected system in your stack that still requires daily manual clicks?

remixes.hook: We have an API bias in how we think about automation. And it's leaving the hardest problems unsolved.
remixes.body:
We have an API bias in how we think about automation. And it's leaving the hardest problems unsolved.

When someone says "automate this," the first question is always: does it have an API? If yes, build. If no, shrug and move on.

But the workflows that burn the most time are almost never the ones with clean API access. They're the ones trapped behind login portals, internal tools, and vendor platforms that peaked in 2007.

I had one of these. A CRM verification step that required manual navigation through a web form with aggressive session timeouts. No API. No CSV export. No webhook. The vendor's "integration guide" was a broken link.

Previous approach: a VA spent 45 minutes a day copying data between screens. Error rate was around 8%.

New approach: Claude computer use logs in, navigates the portal, extracts what I need, handles the timeouts, and writes clean data back to my pipeline. Error rate dropped to under 1%.

The unlock isn't that computer use is better than APIs. It's that it covers the 40% of enterprise workflows that APIs never will. The ugly corners. The forgotten tools. The stuff that works but nobody wants to maintain.

That's where the real automation gap lives. Not in connecting Slack to Notion.

posts.title: Evals are the unsexy moat
posts.hook: Shipped an AI enrichment step that worked perfectly for two weeks. Then it started hallucinating job titles.
posts.body:
Shipped an AI enrichment step that worked perfectly for two weeks. Then it started hallucinating job titles.

No code changes. No prompt changes. The model just drifted. "VP of Revenue" started appearing on contacts who were clearly individual contributors. My pipeline kept running. Kept pushing bad data into sequences.

Caught it because I'd built a dead simple eval: sample 20 enriched records per day, compare the AI output against the LinkedIn profile, log the accuracy score to a CSV.

When accuracy dropped below 85%, a cron job pinged me on Discord.

The fix took 10 minutes. Added a constraint to the prompt and accuracy went back to 94%. But without the eval, I'd have sent 200+ emails to the wrong personas before anyone noticed.

The pattern I keep seeing: teams spend weeks building the agent, zero time building the check. Then they blame the model when the output degrades.

Your eval doesn't need to be fancy. Mine is a Python script, a CSV, and a threshold alert. 40 lines of code. It's caught three drift events in four months.

The agent is the flashy part. The eval is the part that keeps it running.
posts.cta: If you're running AI in any pipeline, what's your drift detection look like?

remixes.label: silent-failure-story
remixes.hook: My AI pipeline ran perfectly for 14 days. On day 15, it started poisoning my CRM. I didn't notice for a week.
remixes.body:
My AI pipeline ran perfectly for 14 days. On day 15, it started poisoning my CRM. I didn't notice for a week.

The enrichment step that maps job titles from LinkedIn data to our internal taxonomy just... shifted. "Individual Contributor" started getting tagged as "VP of Revenue." Not every time. Maybe 15% of records. Just enough to look plausible if you weren't checking.

Those bad records flowed into sequences. SDRs sent personalized emails referencing VP-level pain points to people three levels below. Response rate cratered. One prospect replied asking if we even looked at their profile.

The fix wasn't better prompting. It was building a 30-line eval script that samples 20 records per day and checks them against known ground truth. Title matches the LinkedIn source? Company size in the right band? Role level makes sense given the org chart?

It runs after every enrichment batch. If accuracy drops below 90%, it kills the pipeline and sends me a Slack alert. That's it. No ML. No fancy monitoring platform. Just a cron job and a threshold.

Model drift is real and it doesn't announce itself. Your prompts don't change. Your code doesn't change. The outputs just quietly degrade. If you don't have something watching for it, you're trusting a system that can change without telling you.
remixes.cta: When's the last time you actually spot-checked the output of an AI step in your pipeline?

remixes.label: eval-as-infrastructure
remixes.hook: Your AI pipeline doesn't need better prompts. It needs a 30-line script that tells you when the prompts stop working.
remixes.body:
Your AI pipeline doesn't need better prompts. It needs a 30-line script that tells you when the prompts stop working.

I learned this the hard way. Built an enrichment step that classifies job titles from raw LinkedIn data. Worked great for two weeks. Then the model started drifting. "VP of Revenue" showing up on individual contributors. No code changes on my end. Just quiet degradation.

The records kept flowing into my sequences. Bad data, good formatting. The worst kind of failure because everything looks normal until a prospect replies confused.

So I built the simplest eval I could think of. Sample 20 records per batch. Check title against the LinkedIn source. Check company size against known data. Check role level for obvious mismatches. If accuracy drops below 90%, kill the pipeline.

Total code: 30 lines of Python and a cron job.

This isn't glamorous work. Nobody posts about their eval scripts on LinkedIn. But this is the difference between an AI demo and an AI system. Demos work until they don't. Systems know when they're broken.

The bar isn't perfection. It's awareness. Can your pipeline tell you when it's producing garbage? If the answer is no, you don't have a pipeline. You have a time bomb with good formatting.

posts.title: Context window costs nobody talks about
posts.hook: Ran the numbers on my inference costs after switching to 200k context windows. It was not a fun spreadsheet.
posts.body:
Ran the numbers on my inference costs after switching to 200k context windows. It was not a fun spreadsheet.

I have a content pipeline that processes voice transcripts, checks them against my voice DNA files, and drafts posts. When I started stuffing the full transcript plus all reference docs into one call, the quality went up. The bill went up faster.

$0.47 per run became $3.80 per run. I run it daily. That's $114/month for one pipeline step.

The fix was embarrassingly simple. I split it into two calls. First call: summarize the transcript into key points (short context, cheap). Second call: draft against the summary plus voice DNA (medium context, reasonable).

Total cost dropped to $0.92 per run. Quality stayed the same because the summary preserved everything the drafting step actually needed.

The 200k context window is real and it works. But "can fit" and "should fit" are different questions. Most of the tokens you're stuffing in there are noise the model has to wade through.

Prompt caching helps if you're repeating the same system context. But the bigger lever is just asking: does the model actually need all of this to do its job?
posts.cta: Have you audited your per-call inference costs lately? The numbers might surprise you.

remixes.label: context-window-audit
remixes.hook: I was burning $120/day on inference without realizing it. A two-hour audit cut it to $18.
remixes.body:
I was burning $120/day on inference without realizing it. A two-hour audit cut it to $18.

The problem was lazy context management. I have a content pipeline that processes voice transcripts, checks them against reference docs, and drafts posts. When I built it, I did the obvious thing: stuff everything into one call. Full transcript. All reference files. Voice DNA. Examples.

Quality was great. Cost was $3.80 per run. I run this thing 30+ times a day across different content types. Do the math.

The audit was simple. I logged every call for a week with the full input/output. Then I asked: what's actually being used? Turns out 60% of the reference docs were never relevant to any given run. The full transcript could be chunked, with only relevant sections passed per step.

Three changes: chunked the transcript by section and only passed what was needed per step. Built a simple relevance filter for reference docs. Turned on prompt caching for the stable system prompt.

$3.80 became $0.60. Same output quality based on my eval scores. The model doesn't need everything at once. It needs the right things at the right step.

The pattern I keep seeing: people optimize prompts for quality but never audit prompts for cost. Both matter. Especially when you're running at volume.
remixes.cta: Have you ever logged the actual token count of your AI calls? The bloat is usually worse than you think.

remixes.label: cheap-vs-good-tradeoff
remixes.hook: "Just use the biggest context window" is the new "just throw it in the cloud." Both sound smart until the bill arrives.
remixes.body:
"Just use the biggest context window" is the new "just throw it in the cloud." Both sound smart until the bill arrives.

I fell into this trap with my content pipeline. Processing voice transcripts against reference docs. The easy path: dump everything into a 200k context call and let the model figure it out. Quality was good. I stopped thinking about it.

Then I looked at costs. $0.47 per run had become $3.80 per run. Multiplied across 30+ daily runs, I was spending more on inference than on the tools the pipeline was built to replace.

The fix wasn't switching models or cutting quality. It was being intentional about what goes into each call.

Step one: I split the pipeline into stages. Each stage gets only the context it needs. The drafting step doesn't need the full transcript. The voice check doesn't need the topic research.

Step two: prompt caching. My system prompt and voice DNA files are stable across runs. Caching them cut repeated token costs by 70%.

Step three: I set a per-run cost budget. If a call is going to exceed $1, it gets flagged for review before executing. This forced me to question whether each call actually needed that much context.

Result: per-run cost dropped to $0.55. Quality held. Some steps actually improved because the model wasn't swimming in irrelevant context.

Bigger context windows are a tool, not a strategy. The strategy is knowing exactly what your model needs to see and when.

posts.title: Most AI automation is Zapier with a hat on
posts.hook: Saw someone charge $5,000 for an "AI automation" that was a Zapier workflow with a GPT step in the middle.
posts.body:
Saw someone charge $5,000 for an "AI automation" that was a Zapier workflow with a GPT step in the middle.

Look, Zapier + GPT is fine for some things. Summarize an email, route a form submission, draft a reply. That's legitimate.

But calling it "AI automation" and pricing it like custom software is a different move.

The gap between a Zapier flow and an actual multi-step agent pipeline is enormous:

✅ Zapier flow: trigger --> single LLM call --> output to spreadsheet
✅ Agent pipeline: event watcher --> enrichment --> scoring model --> conditional routing --> CRM write --> sequence enrollment --> eval loop

One is a macro. The other is a system.

I built my outbound pipeline with Python scripts, Claude API calls, SQLite for state management, and cron jobs for orchestration. Total infrastructure cost: $0/month beyond API usage. No Zapier. No Make. No middleware tax.

The real unlock isn't adding AI to your existing no-code stack. It's realizing that a coding agent can build you the actual system in a weekend, and you own every piece of it.

That's the part that makes the middleware vendors nervous.

remixes.label: automation-pricing-gap
remixes.hook: The market hasn't figured out how to price AI work yet. And both buyers and sellers are getting burned.
remixes.body:
The market hasn't figured out how to price AI work yet. And both buyers and sellers are getting burned.

I see two failure modes. On one side: agencies charging $5,000 for a Zapier flow with a GPT step, calling it "AI automation." The client pays enterprise prices for a no-code workflow that breaks when an edge case appears. On the other side: engineers building genuinely complex multi-step agent pipelines and undercharging because they can't articulate the difference.

The gap between these two things is enormous. A Zapier flow is a single decision path with one AI call. An actual agent pipeline has retry logic, error handling, state management, evaluations, fallback routing, and observability. One takes an afternoon. The other takes weeks.

But from the buyer's perspective, they both "use AI." And that's the problem.

I think the fix is specificity in scoping. When I scope AI automation work now, I describe exactly what happens at each step. What triggers it. What data flows where. What happens when it fails. What monitors it. How we know it's working.

Clients who see that level of detail immediately understand why a robust pipeline costs more than a Zapier flow. The ones who don't understand are usually the ones who'd be fine with a Zapier flow anyway.

The market will correct. But right now, if you're building real AI systems, you need to sell the complexity or someone with a no-code tool will underbid you every time.
remixes.cta: How do you scope and price AI automation work differently from traditional software?

remixes.label: when-zapier-breaks
remixes.hook: A Zapier + GPT workflow is fine until the first edge case. Then you learn why code exists.
remixes.body:
A Zapier + GPT workflow is fine until the first edge case. Then you learn why code exists.

I used to run my lead enrichment through a no-code flow. Pull data from Apollo, pass it to GPT for classification, write the result to a sheet. Worked great for the happy path.

Then the edge cases started. A company with no website. A contact with a job title in another language. A response that came back as valid JSON one time and plain text the next. Each edge case needed a workaround. Each workaround made the flow more fragile.

After the fifth "quick fix" I had a Zapier flow with 23 steps, three filter branches, and a prayer. Debugging it meant clicking through a visual interface trying to find which step swallowed the error.

Rewrote it in Python in an afternoon. 80 lines. Try/except around the API calls. Type checking on the GPT output. Logging that actually tells me what happened. Runs as a cron job.

Here's the thing: the Python version isn't smarter. It just handles failure better. No-code tools are optimized for the happy path. Code is optimized for everything else.

This isn't an argument against no-code. It's an argument for knowing when you've outgrown it. If your Zapier flow has more than 10 steps or handles data that's inconsistent, you've probably crossed that line.

posts.title: AI for disqualification not personalization
posts.hook: The best use of AI in my outbound isn't writing better emails. It's killing leads before they enter a sequence.
posts.body:
The best use of AI in my outbound isn't writing better emails. It's killing leads before they enter a sequence.

I built an enrichment step that pulls a company's tech stack, recent job postings, and funding data, then asks Claude one question: "Based on this data, give me three reasons this company would NOT be a fit."

If it finds three strong reasons, the lead gets tagged "disqualified" and never enters outbound. No email. No sequence. No SDR time wasted.

Results after 60 days:

✅ Lead volume into sequences dropped 41%
✅ Reply rate went from 3.2% to 7.8%
✅ Meetings booked stayed flat (same number, fewer sends)
✅ Unsubscribe rate dropped by half

The math is simple. Sending 1,000 emails to get 32 replies is worse than sending 590 emails to get 46 replies. Fewer sends, better deliverability, less domain risk.

Every GTM team I talk to wants AI to write more personalized first lines. Almost none of them are using AI to ask "should we even email this person?"

Disqualification is the higher-leverage problem. Your domain reputation will thank you.
posts.cta: What signals do you use to kill a lead before it hits a sequence?

remixes.label: negative-signal-stack
remixes.hook: I added a disqualification layer to my outbound pipeline. Reply rates went up 40% and I'm sending fewer emails.
remixes.body:
I added a disqualification layer to my outbound pipeline. Reply rates went up 40% and I'm sending fewer emails.

The math is simple. If 30% of your leads are bad fits, every email to them is noise. Worse, it's noise that trains spam filters, tanks your domain reputation, and wastes sequence slots.

So I built a negative signal stack. Before any lead enters a sequence, it goes through three checks.

First, tech stack mismatch. If they're running a competitor or a tool that makes our offering redundant, they're out. I pull this from job postings and BuiltWith data.

Second, timing signals. Recently laid off their sales team? Just closed a round and haven't hired yet? In the middle of a platform migration? Bad timing is worse than bad fit. These leads get tagged "revisit in 90 days" instead of disqualified.

Third, the Claude check. I feed the enriched profile to Claude and ask one question: "Give me three reasons this company would NOT be a good fit." If it finds three strong reasons backed by data, the lead gets killed.

The counterintuitive part: the leads that survive all three checks convert at nearly double the rate. Not because the messaging is better. Because the audience is better.

Most outbound optimization focuses on what to say. The bigger lever is who to say it to. And the fastest way to improve who is to get better at saying no.
remixes.cta: What's your strongest disqualification signal? The one that saves you the most wasted sequences?

remixes.label: anti-personalization-take
remixes.hook: Stop using AI to personalize outbound. Start using it to delete leads.
remixes.body:
Stop using AI to personalize outbound. Start using it to delete leads.

The default AI outbound playbook right now: enrich a lead, generate a personalized first line, send it. Everyone's doing this. Which means everyone's inbox looks the same. "I saw you recently posted about X" written by a model that saw the same LinkedIn post as every other AI tool.

Personalization is a race to the bottom when everyone has the same tools.

Disqualification is the opposite. It's using AI to make your list smaller and better before you write a single word.

I have an enrichment step that pulls tech stack, job postings, and funding data for every lead. Then Claude answers one question: why would this company NOT buy? If it finds three strong, data-backed reasons, the lead never enters a sequence.

The result: I'm sending maybe 60% of the emails I used to send. Reply rates are up significantly. Not because the emails are better. Because every email goes to someone who actually has a reason to care.

The best cold email you can write is no email to the wrong person.

Every AI-written first line you send to a bad-fit lead is doing negative work. It costs tokens, burns send reputation, and takes a sequence slot from someone who might have replied.

Flip the script. Use AI to find reasons NOT to reach out. Your pipeline will thank you.

posts.title: Document mistakes not thought leadership
posts.hook: My highest-performing LinkedIn post last quarter was about a pipeline I broke at 2am on a Sunday.
posts.body:
My highest-performing LinkedIn post last quarter was about a pipeline I broke at 2am on a Sunday.

I accidentally pushed a schema change that dropped a column my enrichment script depended on. 400+ leads got processed with blank company data. Half of them went into sequences with personalization that referenced... nothing.

"Hey {{first_name}}, saw that {{company}} is..."

Yeah. That went out.

I wrote about the whole thing. The root cause (no migration safeguard on the SQLite table), the blast radius (3 sequences, ~180 emails before I caught it), and the fix (added a pre-send validation that checks for empty merge fields).

That post did 4x my normal engagement. Not because failure is entertaining, though it is. Because it was specific. People could see exactly what went wrong and steal the fix for their own stack.

Thought leadership is mostly pattern matching on what performed last week, rewritten with slightly different words. Mistake documentation is unique by definition. Nobody else broke your specific thing in your specific way.

The irony is that the posts where I feel least polished are the ones that perform best. The audience can tell the difference between "I thought about this" and "this happened to me."

remixes.body:
I keep a public failure log. Every broken pipeline, every bad deploy, every email that went out with {{company}} in the subject line.

Not because I enjoy the embarrassment. Because every time I post one of these, three things happen.

First, someone DMs me saying they had the exact same problem and felt alone. Second, I get replies with solutions I hadn't considered. Third, my engagement outperforms my polished "here's how I did it" posts by 3x or more.

The reason is simple. Thought leadership is a crowded lane. Everyone has frameworks, mental models, and hot takes about where the market is going. Very few people are posting the screenshot of the Slack message where they told their client that 400 leads got garbage data because they forgot to test a schema migration.

Failure content works because it signals something that polished content can't: that you actually do the work. Anyone can write "5 Tips for Better Outbound." Not everyone can describe exactly how their enrichment pipeline failed at 2am and what they changed the next morning to prevent it.

The vulnerability isn't the point. The specificity is. When you describe a real mistake in real detail, readers learn more in 200 words than they do from a 2,000 word best practices guide.

Document the mess. The audience already knows the work is messy. They're waiting for someone to say it out loud.
remixes.cta: What's the last thing you broke that you could turn into a post today?

remixes.label: contrarian-flip
remixes.hook: Stop writing about what you know. Start writing about what you got wrong.
remixes.body:
Stop writing about what you know. Start writing about what you got wrong.

I ran an experiment last quarter. I alternated between two types of LinkedIn posts. Week one: a clean, polished breakdown of a workflow I built. Week two: a raw account of something I screwed up.

The failure posts won every single time. More impressions, more comments, more DMs that led to actual conversations.

Here's why I think this works. LinkedIn is drowning in expertise performance. Everyone's an expert. Everyone has a framework. The feed is wall to wall confidence.

So when someone posts "I pushed a bad schema change and 400 leads got blank personalization," it breaks the pattern. Readers stop scrolling because it feels real. They engage because they've been there. They DM because they want to talk to someone who won't judge them for making mistakes too.

The irony is that failure content actually builds more authority than thought leadership content. Because it proves you operate. You can't describe a specific production failure if you're not running production systems.

Most people's content strategy is backwards. They hide the mess and broadcast the wins. Flip it. The mess is the content. The wins are just receipts.

posts.title: Treat your GTM stack like a product
posts.hook: My outbound stack has a changelog. Seriously.
posts.body:
My outbound stack has a changelog. Seriously.

Every time I change an enrichment source, swap a scoring threshold, update a prompt, or modify a sequence trigger, it gets logged. Date, what changed, why, and what the expected impact is.

Started doing this after I spent two hours debugging a reply rate drop that turned out to be a prompt change I made three weeks earlier and forgot about.

The pattern I'm seeing with teams that actually win at outbound:

✅ Version-controlled prompts (not edited live in a UI)
✅ Staged rollouts (test new enrichment on 50 leads before running 5,000)
✅ Rollback capability (can revert to last week's scoring model in one command)
✅ Observability (know your reply rate, bounce rate, and enrichment accuracy daily, not monthly)

This is just software engineering applied to GTM. But most RevOps teams treat their stack like a set of disconnected tools instead of a system they're responsible for.

When your outbound breaks, can you git blame it? Can you diff this week's pipeline against last week's?

If the answer is no, you don't have a system. You have a collection of logins.

remixes.body:
I lost two hours last month debugging a reply rate drop. The root cause was a prompt change I made three weeks earlier.

Reply rates dropped from 4.2% to 1.8%. I checked deliverability. Fine. Checked list quality. Same sources. Checked send times, subject lines, sequence structure. All unchanged.

Turns out I'd tweaked the AI prompt that generates the first line of personalization. Small change. Made the output slightly more formal. I'd forgotten about it completely.

That's when I started keeping a changelog for my GTM stack.

Every change gets a line item. Date, what I changed, why, and what metric I expect it to affect. It takes maybe 90 seconds per entry. And it's saved me hours of debugging at least four times since.

The problem with modern GTM stacks is that they have too many moving parts for anyone to hold in their head. posts.title: 4-day SaaS build is real but incomplete
posts.hook: You can ship a SaaS product in 4 days with Claude Code. You cannot ship a business in 4 days.
posts.body:
You can ship a SaaS product in 4 days with Claude Code. You cannot ship a business in 4 days.

I've built and deployed full working apps in a weekend. Auth, database, UI, payment integration. Claude Code handles the scaffolding faster than any workflow I've used.

But the app is maybe 15% of the work.

The other 85%:

✅ Figuring out who actually needs this (not who you think needs it)
✅ Getting 10 people to use it and tell you what's broken
✅ Rewriting the onboarding three times because nobody understands your UI
✅ Learning that your pricing is wrong from the first 5 churns
✅ Building the GTM motion that puts it in front of the right people daily

I built Clearbox's first working prototype in a weekend. The product you see today looks nothing like that prototype. Eight months of user feedback reshaped every major decision.

Coding agents compress the build cycle, which is genuinely powerful. But they don't compress the learning cycle. You still have to sit with users, watch them get confused, and rebuild.

The 4-day build story is inspiring. Just don't confuse shipping code with shipping a company.

The app is 15% of the work. I keep learning this the hard way.

I've shipped three products in the last year using Claude Code. Each time, I had a working app, auth, database, payments, UI, deployed and functional, within a week.

Each time, the real work started after that.

Product one: took six weeks after launch to figure out that my target user wasn't who I thought it was. Rebuilt the onboarding three times.

Product two: shipped fast, got signups, watched everyone churn in week two because the core workflow had friction I couldn't see from inside the builder's perspective.

Product three: finally spent time talking to people before building. The app took four days. The conversations that shaped what to build took three weeks.

AI coding tools have made the building part almost trivially fast. And that's genuinely amazing. But it's created a dangerous illusion that the hard part of software is the software.

The hard parts haven't changed. Who is this for. What problem does it actually solve. Why would they pay for this instead of the 30 other options. How do you reach them. How do you make them stay.

None of those questions get answered by a faster build cycle. They get answered by talking to humans, watching them use your thing, and iterating on the parts that aren't code.

The 4-day SaaS build is real. The 4-day SaaS business is a fantasy.

AI coding tools might be the worst thing to happen to first-time founders.

Not because the tools are bad. They're incredible. Claude Code, Cursor, Copilot. You can ship a real, working product in days instead of months.

The problem is what that speed does to your psychology.

When building was slow, you were forced to validate before you built. You'd spend weeks talking to customers, mapping the market, testing positioning. Because the cost of building the wrong thing was months of wasted development time.

Now the cost of building the wrong thing is a weekend. So people skip validation entirely. Why talk to customers when you can just ship and see what happens?

Here's what happens: you launch, get some traffic, nobody sticks around, and you pivot to building the next thing. Repeat until burnout.

I've done this myself. Built and deployed a full app in 4 days. Auth, database, payments, the works. Felt amazing. Then spent the next two months trying to figure out who actually needed it and why nobody was retaining.

The build speed is a gift. But it only matters if you already know what to build. And knowing what to build still takes the same amount of customer conversations it always did.

Faster tools don't fix unclear thinking. They just let you ship unclear thinking to production faster.

posts.title: SDR team size is the wrong metric
posts.hook: Cutting your SDR team from 8 to 3 isn't an AI story. It's a targeting story.
posts.body:
Cutting your SDR team from 8 to 3 isn't an AI story. It's a targeting story.

I've seen this pattern three times now. Company has a big SDR team. Reply rates are low. They layer in AI tooling, shrink the team, and pipeline goes up.

But when you dig in, the AI didn't write better emails. It forced them to define their ICP for the first time. Because when you're feeding data into a scoring model, you have to articulate what a good account actually looks like. You can't just say "mid-market SaaS" anymore.

The 5 SDRs who got cut were sending to accounts that never should have been in the pipeline. The AI was the forcing function, not the fix.

This is why I'm skeptical of "AI replaced X headcount" narratives. In most cases, the company had a targeting problem disguised as a capacity problem. AI just made the targeting problem impossible to ignore.

The real question isn't "can AI do what my SDRs do?" It's "should my SDRs have been doing that work in the first place?"

If 60% of your outbound was going to accounts that would never buy, you didn't have an efficiency problem. You had a strategy problem.
posts.cta: How much of your current outbound volume is going to accounts that realistically will never close?

remixes.label: hidden-variable
remixes.hook: The AI didn't write better cold emails. It forced the team to define their ICP for the first time.
remixes.body:
The AI didn't write better cold emails. It forced the team to define their ICP for the first time.

I've watched this play out three times now. Company has 8 SDRs. Reply rates are flat. They bring in AI tooling, shrink the team to 3, and pipeline goes up.

The vendor says it's the AI. The case study says it's the AI. Everyone on LinkedIn says it's the AI.

But when you look at what actually changed, it's the targeting.

Because when you feed data into a scoring model, you can't be vague about what a good account looks like. You have to define criteria. Revenue range, tech stack, hiring signals, funding stage. You have to make explicit decisions that used to live in a rep's gut.

The 8-person team was sending to everyone who loosely fit the vertical. The 3-person team is sending to a filtered, scored, prioritized list. Of course the numbers are better. You subtracted the waste.

The AI is useful. I'm not arguing it isn't. But the leverage came from the constraint it imposed. When you have fewer people, you can't afford to spray. You're forced to aim.

Most SDR teams don't have a headcount problem. They have a targeting problem that headcount has been masking. Cut the volume, define the criteria, and the team size question answers itself.
remixes.cta: If you scored every account your SDRs touched last quarter, what percentage would actually match your ICP?

remixes.label: math-proof
remixes.hook: 8 SDRs sending 200 emails a day to a vague list will always lose to 3 SDRs sending 50 emails to the right accounts.
remixes.body:
8 SDRs sending 200 emails a day to a vague list will always lose to 3 SDRs sending 50 emails to the right accounts.

Let's do the math.

Team A: 8 reps, 200 sends each, 1,600 emails per day. Reply rate: 1.2%. That's 19 replies. Maybe 4 are positive. Of those, 1 converts to a meeting.

Team B: 3 reps, 50 sends each, 150 emails per day. Reply rate: 6%. That's 9 replies. 5 are positive. 3 convert to meetings.

Team B sends 90% less volume and books 3x the meetings. The difference isn't AI, copywriting, or send times. It's that Team B only emails accounts that match a defined, scored ICP.

I keep seeing companies frame their "AI transformation" as a headcount story. We replaced 5 SDRs with AI. But the real transformation was that they finally stopped sending emails to accounts that were never going to buy.

The SDR team size was never the problem. The targeting was. The big team existed to compensate for bad targeting with more volume. More reps, more sends, more activity metrics that look productive but produce nothing.

Shrinking the team works because it forces a constraint. You can't spray when you only have 3 people. You have to prioritize. And prioritization requires defining who actually buys your product.

The question isn't how many SDRs do you need. It's how many accounts genuinely match your ICP. Start there.

posts.title: Build in public means the messy middle
posts.hook: Week 8 of building Clearbox in public, I posted that I had zero paying users and wasn't sure the product worked.
posts.body:
Week 8 of building Clearbox in public, I posted that I had zero paying users and wasn't sure the product worked.

That post got more DMs than anything I'd shipped before it. Three of those DMs became design partners. Two of those design partners became paying customers.

The build-in-public posts that actually work aren't the MRR screenshots. They're the ones where you say "I built this thing and I don't know if anyone wants it yet."

Because that's relatable. Every builder has been there. And when you're honest about it, the people who respond are the ones who actually care about the problem you're solving. They're not congratulating you. They're saying "I have that problem too."

The MRR update is a scoreboard. The messy middle is a conversation.

I track my build-in-public cadence the same way I track outbound metrics. What got replies? What got DMs? What turned into a call? The pattern is consistent: vulnerability plus specificity outperforms polish plus numbers.

"Here's what broke and how I fixed it" beats "hit $3k MRR" every time. Not in likes. In pipeline.

If you're building in public to get followers, post the wins. If you're building in public to get customers, post the problems.

remixes.body:
The DMs that turned into customers didn't come from my launch post. They came from the post where I admitted I wasn't sure the product worked.

Week 8 of building Clearbox in public. Zero paying users. Core feature still felt half-baked. I could have posted another progress update with a clean screenshot and a "shipping fast" caption. Instead I wrote the truth.

The post said, roughly: I built this thing. I've been showing it to people. Some of them think it's interesting. None of them have paid for it. I'm not sure if that means the product is wrong, the positioning is wrong, or I just haven't found the right buyer yet.

Three DMs within 24 hours. All some version of: "I'm dealing with the same problem you're trying to solve. Can I see it?"

Two of those became design partners. Both became paying customers.

Here's why I think this works. When you post wins, you attract spectators. When you post uncertainty, you attract people who share the problem. Spectators like your post. People with the problem DM you.

The build-in-public content that drives revenue isn't the MRR chart or the feature announcement. It's the honest update where you admit you don't have it figured out yet. Because that's the signal that tells your future customer: this person is building for real, and they might actually listen to what I need.

remixes.hook: I've tracked which build-in-public posts generate DMs vs. likes. The pattern is consistent and counterintuitive.
remixes.body:
I've tracked which build-in-public posts generate DMs vs. likes. The pattern is consistent and counterintuitive.

Posts that get likes: MRR milestones, clean product screenshots, "just shipped" announcements, progress threads with green checkmarks.

Posts that get DMs: admitting a feature doesn't work yet, sharing that nobody's paying, asking whether the positioning is wrong, documenting a pivot in real time.

The likes posts build audience. The DMs posts build pipeline.

Week 8 of Clearbox, I posted that I had zero paying users and wasn't sure the product worked. That post got more DMs than any launch or milestone update. Three became design partners. Two became paying customers.
